description: The sqlivuln() function constructs a SQL query using an f-string with unsanitized user input. The password parameter is accepted but never used in the WHERE clause, meaning authentication is bypassed entirely — only the username field is checked, and it is injectable.
exploitation_scenario: POST /api/sqlivuln with body {"username": "' OR '1'='1", "password": "anything"}. The resulting query becomes SELECT * FROM USERS WHERE USERNAME='' OR '1'='1' which returns all rows. Full dump: {"username": "' UNION SELECT name,sql FROM sqlite_master--", "password": "x"} leaks schema.
suggested_fix: Use parameterized queries: cur.execute('SELECT * FROM USERS WHERE USERNAME=? AND PASSWORD=?', (username, password))

description: sstivuln() concatenates raw user input directly into a Jinja2 Template string. Jinja2 evaluates the template, so any template expression in the input is executed server-side. This leads to Remote Code Execution.
exploitation_scenario: POST /api/sstivuln with body {"mathexp": "{{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read()}}"}. Server returns the output of the 'id' shell command. Full shell: replace with 'cat /etc/passwd' or a reverse shell payload.
suggested_fix: Never concatenate user input into a template string. Use Template with variables instead: Template('my temp: {{ exp }}').render(exp=exp) — this treats user input as data, not template code.

description: lfivuln() passes the user-supplied filename directly to open() with no path restriction, canonicalization, or allowlist. Any file readable by the process can be retrieved, including /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, application source files, and private keys.
exploitation_scenario: POST /api/lfivuln with body {"filename": "/etc/passwd"} returns the full passwd file. {"filename": "../../etc/shadow"} attempts shadow passwords. {"filename": "/proc/self/environ"} leaks environment variables including any secrets.
suggested_fix: Enforce an allowlist of permitted filenames or restrict reads to a safe base directory: base = '/app/safe_files'; path = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(base, filename)); assert path.startswith(base)

description: rfivuln() makes an outbound HTTP request to any URL supplied by the user with no allowlist, scheme restriction, or host validation. SSL certificate verification is also disabled (verify=False). This enables SSRF to internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, and localhost, plus MITM on any HTTPS target.
exploitation_scenario: POST /api/rfivuln with body {"imagelink": "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/"} retrieves AWS IAM credentials. {"imagelink": "http://localhost:6379/"} probes Redis. {"imagelink": "file:///etc/passwd"} may work depending on the requests version.
suggested_fix: Validate the URL against an allowlist of permitted hosts/schemes. Reject private IP ranges (RFC 1918, 169.254.x.x, ::1). Remove verify=False and enforce TLS. Use a DNS rebinding-resistant library.

description: hhivuln() reads the Host request header and reflects it unsanitized into an HTML <a href='...'> attribute in the JSON response. An attacker controlling the Host header can inject arbitrary URLs, enabling phishing via password reset links, cache poisoning, and open redirects.
exploitation_scenario: Send POST /api/hhivuln with header 'Host: evil.com' — response contains <a href='evil.com'>. In a password-reset flow this would generate a reset link pointing to the attacker's server, harvesting tokens. With XSS: Host: x' onmouseover='alert(1) creates a stored/reflected XSS vector.
suggested_fix: Never use the Host header to construct URLs. Use a configured server-side base URL. If the Host header must be used, validate it against an allowlist of permitted domains.

description: The Flask application starts with debug=True and binds to 0.0.0.0. In debug mode, Werkzeug enables an interactive Python debugger on exception pages. If the PIN is predictable (e.g., in containerized environments with fixed /proc/self/cgroup values), the debugger console allows arbitrary code execution.
exploitation_scenario: Trigger an unhandled exception at any endpoint. The Werkzeug debugger appears. The PIN can be computed from /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id, /proc/self/cgroup, and the MAC address — all leaked via the LFI vulnerability above — giving full RCE on the host.
suggested_fix: Set debug=False in production. Use an environment variable: debug=os.getenv('FLASK_DEBUG', 'false').lower() == 'true'. Never bind 0.0.0.0 in production without a reverse proxy.

description: When a SQL exception occurs (e.g., from a malformed injection attempt), the raw SQLite exception message is returned verbatim in the JSON response: {"msg": "<sqlite error>"}. This leaks table names, column names, and query structure to attackers.
exploitation_scenario: POST /api/sqlivuln with body {"username": "'", "password": "x"} — the unmatched quote triggers a SQLite parse error that names the table and column involved, giving an attacker the schema needed to craft precise injections.
suggested_fix: Catch exceptions and return a generic error message: return {"msg": "Login failed"}, 401. Log the real error server-side only.

description: Plaintext credentials (mike:kaines and admin:admin) are hardcoded directly in the database initialization script. Anyone with source access has the full credential set. The admin account uses a trivially guessable password.
exploitation_scenario: Read custom_db.py (via LFI or source access) to obtain credentials. POST /api/sqlivuln with {"username": "admin", "password": "admin"} authenticates immediately. The mike:kaines credential also works.
suggested_fix: Never hardcode credentials. Load initial credentials from environment variables or a secrets manager. Hash passwords with bcrypt/argon2 before storing.

description: The reflected() function returns the username value verbatim in a JSON response without HTML encoding. The Swagger UI (served by connexion at /ui/) renders API responses in a browser context. A crafted payload in the username field can execute JavaScript when the response is viewed through the Swagger UI.
exploitation_scenario: POST /api/xssreflected with body {"username": ""}. If the Swagger UI or any downstream consumer renders this as HTML, the XSS fires and can steal session cookies or perform actions as the victim.
suggested_fix: HTML-encode output: from markupsafe import escape; return {"msg": f"Hello, {escape(username)}"}, 200. For JSON APIs, set Content-Type: application/json and ensure consumers parse as JSON, not HTML.

description: requests.get() is called with verify=False, disabling TLS certificate validation for all outbound HTTPS requests. Combined with the SSRF vulnerability, this means an attacker can direct the server to fetch HTTPS URLs from attacker-controlled infrastructure without certificate validation, enabling MITM interception of the fetched content.
exploitation_scenario: Set up an HTTPS server with a self-signed cert at attacker.com. POST /api/rfivuln with {"imagelink": "https://internal-service/secret-token"}. Position MITM between server and internal-service. Since verify=False, the MITM certificate is accepted and the secret is intercepted.
suggested_fix: Remove verify=False. Use verify=True (the default). If custom CA certs are needed, use verify='/path/to/ca-bundle.crt'.
